title: Algorithms: The Loops You Should Not Write

questions.question: What does end() point at?
options: One position past the last element
The last element
The first element
Nothing, it is always null
questions.explanation: That is why begin() to end() visits every element exactly once, and why a search returning end() means not found rather than pointing at something.

questions.question: What does std::remove_if do to a container's size?
options: Nothing. It shuffles the keepers to the front and returns the new end
It shrinks the container to fit
It sets the removed elements to a default value
It reallocates the container
questions.explanation: It only has iterators, and iterators cannot resize a container. The erase call is what actually shortens it, and calling remove_if alone reports no error.

questions.question: What is wrong with std::accumulate(begin, end, 0) over temperatures?
options: The starting value makes every addition integer, so each step truncates
It cannot accumulate structs
It starts from the wrong end
Nothing, 0 is the correct starting value
questions.explanation: The type of the initial value is the type of the accumulator. Writing 0.0 instead of 0 is the whole fix, and the compiler accepts either without complaint.

questions.question: Why must a comparator for std::sort be false for equal elements?
options: Otherwise an element counts as before itself and the sort walks off the end of the range
Because sorting would be unstable
Because equal elements would be removed
So the sort can run in parallel
questions.explanation: The partition step hunts a pivot that cannot exist, and the result is a heap buffer overflow deep inside the standard library, which is the crash triaged in lesson 04-02.

questions.question: Why is a named algorithm usually better than the equivalent loop?
options: It states what is being done, and the bounds are not yours to get wrong
It always runs faster
It uses less memory
It works on containers that loops cannot handle
questions.explanation: The name carries the intent, and the off by one that a hand written loop invites simply cannot be written.

questions.question: After std::find_if, what must happen before reading the result?
options: Compare it against end(), because dereferencing end() is undefined behaviour
Check that the container is not empty
Convert it to an index
Nothing, the result is always valid
questions.explanation: It is exactly the null pointer check in different clothing: the not found answer is a value that must never be dereferenced.
